The "Physics" in Babylon.js is at the inexcusably 'my first game engine' level of incompetence... velocity and acceleration are treated as if they have the same dimensions... lacks understanding of world time.
As a technical 3D artist, Babylon has been a great way to dive into web dev, and it parallels with standard game engines just enough that I can easily find my way around the documentation.
Babylon is amazing, the documentation and backwards compatibility is quite something. Just finished a project with it, while the learning curve is steep, it doesn't blindside you.
Babylon.js is (working towards) being a batteries included game engine... A better comparison for Babylon.js is Playcanvas.

ThreeJS's API breaks backwards compatibility a lot, while Babylon is exactly the opposite. Babylon also has vastly superior documentation and doesn't seem to suffer from lag spikes as much. However, it's three times the size of ThreeJS, so bandwidth optimization is required.

I've tried babylon.js. My gripes: no 'preferred navigation feel', setting up a basic sky/ground scene is worse than HTML from 25 years ago, and I never found any active community using babylon.js outside MS-run channels.

three.js seems to be more well known/established than babylon... I went with babylon and i'm glad i did. It has better performance and the object names and concepts seemed easier to follow and a little less obtuse.
I switched my current project from Three to Babylon about two years ago... Babylon has a compact, active set of devs (I've made bug reports and seen the fix in the next nightly build multiple times).
Babylon.js is an amazing framework. The 3d concepts are ingrained into the API and framework. The ability to read 3d model data from Blender and things just work is awesome.
The impressive thing about Babylon.js is Spector — a fully functional WebGL debugger extension in Chrome which makes 3D development on the web so much easier, works with Three.js too!
Babylon.js works in all 3 of the major browsers, and performs best in Firefox, not IE10.
It seems to be pretty heavy on object allocation, e.g. BABYLON.Vector3.prototype.add creates a new Vector3 each call, unlike gl-matrix's in-place operations — constant allocation risks GC pauses.
Version 1.2 is out :) [disclaimer: I'm the author] Major rework of the API to remove GC pressure.
This has so many more capabilities than Three.js and the gap seems to be growing.
Babylon is awesome! I just started writing a game with it. The integration with TypeScript works well and there also are fun things like React-BabylonJS.

I built a 3rd-person MMORPG using Babylon v4.0... but questioned why bother with a strictly web-based engine for a complex game, and ported to Godot instead. Babylon is great for web 3D content but not ideal for a significant standalone game.

demos look quite nice but wow they take a long time to load, took about 5 minutes to download 50mb for a short scene, makes me wonder if download times are going to be a limiting factor in webgl games.

I decided to start developing a 3rd-person MMORPG using Babylon v4.0... after investing far too much time I came to question why I was bothering with a strictly web-based engine... halted dev on the babylon version and begun porting to Godot. Babylon is a great choice for web-based 3d content, but for a significant game I'd recommend a proper game engine from the start.

To avoid having too long loading time, we have support for incremental loading. But we definitely need to work on optimizing the size of our scene format also.
